transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-04-07 16:30 UTC | Duration: 47 minutes | Recording: yes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Morales (Redwood SE), Lena Park (NorthForge CTO), Marc Ruiz (NorthForge Head of Cloud), Priya Sethi (Integration Lead)

Summary: quick partner intro; NorthForge is exploring an edge adaptor to route inference workloads from their on-prem appliances into Redwood Dedicated pools or a private on-prem runtime. Primary asks: integration pattern, security controls (KMS, SSO, audit), and pilot framing with throughput/latency goals.

Topics: partner integration pattern, VPC / on-prem connectivity, GPU footprint and bench targets, compliance (SOC2/ISO), pilot scope and timeline, commercial model (reseller vs referral).

-- Transcript --
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, uh thanks for joining — we're excited to talk through how Redwood can fit into NorthForge's edge adaptor story. Quick round of intros?
[00:12] Lena Park: Hi I'm Lena, CTO at NorthForge. We build edge appliances for telco and retail customers, and we're looking at how to surface LLM features without shipping everything to cloud.
[00:23] Marc Ruiz: Marc here, I run cloud eng. Priya's on the call she'll lead integrations.
[00:29] Priya Sethi: Hey all.
[00:31] Diego Morales: Diego, Redwood SE, I focus on private deployments and high-throughput serving.
[00:36] Maya Chen: Great, thanks. I'll pass to Diego to frame the integration patterns we commonly do.
[00:41] Diego Morales: Cool — so there are basically three ways teams usually integrate: one is full hosted API traffic (for non-sensitive payloads), two is Redwood Dedicated where you reserve GPU capacity in our infra, and three is Redwood Private - VPC or on-prem control plane — which sounds like what you're leaning to, correct?
[00:58] Lena Park: Right, we can't push certain PII off-device for some customers. We like the idea of a private control plane or even an on-prem runtime wrapped in our appliance.
[01:09] Marc Ruiz: Two quick constraints: first, many of our appliances are behind strict NATs and intermittent connectivity, so persistent bi-directional tunnels are tricky. Second, we try to optimize for 80ms p99 for small prompts.
[01:23] Diego Morales: Understood. For NAT/intermittent nets we often use an outbound-only egress model with a long-lived TLS tunnel to Redwood gateway or an edge adaptor that buffers and batches requests locally and forwards to Dedicated pools. That adaptor can also run a lightweight quantized model if latency requirement is super tight.
[01:41] Priya Sethi: So adaptor = runs on the appliance, does local batching, KV cache, then routes to Redwood when connectivity is up. Does it support switching to local model if no link?
[01:53] Diego Morales: Yes, that's exactly the pattern. You can have a fallback tiny model on-device. Redwood's runtime supports prefix caching and continuous batching so when connectivity resumes it drains the queue efficiently. Note transcription: "kay v cache" in some earlier doc — it's actually KV cache.
[02:08] Lena Park: Ha yeah saw that typo in the quickstart.
[02:11] Maya Chen: On security — we support KMS integrations (Cloud KMS, customer HSMs), SSO via SAML/OIDC, RBAC for routes, and audit logs. Marc, does audit log retention need to be on-prem?
[02:26] Marc Ruiz: For some customers yes, logs must be retained in their region and we need proof of access controls for audits.
[02:33] Diego Morales: We can push logs to your SIEM over secure channels, and Private can be deployed entirely in your VPC so logs never leave your network. For on-prem we have an air-gapped package but it's heavier — requires on-site install support.
[02:47] Priya Sethi: What's the uplift on latency if we go through Dedicated vs local on-device fallback? Ballpark numbers?
[02:55] Diego Morales: If you're on-device fallback: sub-10ms for tiny models, but accuracy is limited. Hitting Dedicated in-region you're looking at ~30–80ms p50 depending on model and instance type; p95/p99 will vary — we can tune batch sizes for each route. For high throughput we recommend our Dedicated reserved pools to keep per-request queuing minimal.
[03:17] Lena Park: Our main use-case: interactive chat-like assistant that needs p99 < 120ms end-to-end, and QPS per appliance is modest (0.5–2 qps). Aggregated at regional hub could be 500–1k QPS.
[03:33] Marc Ruiz: Also curious about model variants — we run some open models internally. Can Redwood route to customer-managed model images or do we need to use Redwood-curated models?
[03:44] Diego Morales: On Private deployments you can bring-your-own-model (BYOM) — you can run your own containerized model artifact and Redwood runtime will serve it. For hosted/Dedicated we serve our curated catalog but we can support private model images via Dedicated bring-your-own in certain arrangements.
[03:59] Maya Chen: We should flag licensing and model support — some models require special infra, and quantization can change behavior. Diego will follow up with recommended quantization profiles.
[04:09] Priya Sethi: Nice. Another concern: network outages — we can't have customers waiting for 10s of seconds. Buffering is ok but what about prioritization / throttling?
[04:19] Diego Morales: The adaptor can implement local priority queues and token-bucket shaping. Also Redwood Optimize can suggest batching and cache settings per workload to hit latency vs cost sweet spot.
[04:30] Lena Park: On compliance: SOC2 + ISO 27001 are must-haves. We'll need the SOC2 report and an architecture diagram for our security review.
[04:39] Maya Chen: We'll send the SOC2 cert and our security whitepaper.
[04:42] Marc Ruiz: Perfect. Now commercial — are you thinking reseller revenue share if NorthForge bundles Redwood for appliance customers?
[04:50] Maya Chen: We have flexible partner programs — reseller or referral, plus technical enablement. For large committed Dedicated capacity we do co-selling motions and margin. We can introduce our partner ops team later.
[05:03] Priya Sethi: For the pilot we want a simple POC: deploy adaptor in our lab, route to Redwood Dedicated in a sandbox, run synthetic load (500 QPS aggregate) and measure p50/p95/p99, cost per token, and failure modes. If that looks good, we'll scope an on-prem variant.
[05:21] Diego Morales: Sounds good. We'll draft a pilot runbook: test vectors, measurement scripts, required infra (GPU types, instance counts), expected timelines.
[05:28] Lena Park: Timeline - we need an initial pilot in the next 3–4 weeks to align with a sales opportunity. Is that feasible?
[05:35] Maya Chen: Yes we can aim for pilot kickoff week of 2026-04-20. Diego: can you check capacity?
[05:40] Diego Morales: I'll confirm Dedicated pool availability and reserve test instances. Also will include a lightweight on-prem package option for benching.
[05:48] Marc Ruiz: Also, small ask — can you share a simple network diagram showing traffic flows for outbound-only tunnels and what endpoints need to be reachable? Our infra team is stickly about firewall rules.
[05:58] Diego Morales: For sure — we'll attach a diagram to the deck. The typical port is 443 over TLS to a Redwood gateway, and we support mutual TLS if you prefer mTLS.
[06:08] Priya Sethi: Any licensing or SDKs for the adaptor? Do you have a reference implementation?
[06:14] Maya Chen: We have a lightweight reference adaptor repo and some example configs. We'll share links after the call.
[06:19] Marc Ruiz: Competitors — we've also talked to Aurora Compute about similar onramp. Two reasons we like Redwood so far: clearer private deploy options and more mature routing/fallback story.
[06:30] Maya Chen: Appreciate that. We also track per-route cost and latency in the console which helps you tune the economics.
[06:36] Lena Park: Side question on data residency: some customers force data to stay within country boundaries. Can Private be deployed per-country?
[06:43] Diego Morales: Yes, Private can be instantiated in-country VPCs or on-prem. We'll need to run through packaging and support SLAs — on-prem installs have different support windows.
[06:53] Priya Sethi: Ok let's recap the next steps quickly.
[06:56] Maya Chen: Recap: 1) Maya will send the partner deck, security whitepaper, and link to the adaptor repo by 2026-04-09; 2) Marc will share QPS targets and latency SLOs by 2026-04-14; 3) Diego to draft pilot runbook and check Dedicated test capacity by 2026-04-16; 4) schedule pilot kickoff for week of 2026-04-20.
[07:18] Marc Ruiz: That works for us. Priya and I will sync on the infra notes and get the firewall rules list to Diego.
[07:24] Maya Chen: Great — we'll also add a short proposed commercial sketch (reseller vs referral and pilot pricing) in the deck.
[07:31] Lena Park: Thanks everyone, that was helpful.
[07:33] Priya Sethi: Thanks.
[07:35] Diego Morales: Thanks — we'll follow up with the materials.
[07:38] Maya Chen: End call.

References shared during call: partner deck (link: https://redwood.ai/partners/northforge-deck), adaptor repo (link: https://github.com/redwood-inference/edge-adaptor-examples), security whitepaper (link: https://redwood.ai/security/whitepaper.pdf)
